papers.title: Ban the Box, Criminal Records, and Racial Discrimination: A Field Experiment
takeaways: Correspondence experiment: ~15,000 fictitious online applications to employers in New Jersey and New York City, before and after Ban-the-Box adoption, randomising distinctly Black vs distinctly white names and felony conviction status.
Criminal records are a real barrier — employers who asked about them were 63% more likely to call back an applicant with no record.
But removing the box widened the racial gap sharply: at those employers the white-over-Black callback advantage went from 7% to 43%.
The authors read this as employers substituting exaggerated beliefs about racial differences in conviction rates for the information they no longer have.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 2 — discrimination in hiring.

papers.title: The Effect of Job Loss and Unemployment Insurance on Crime in Brazil
papers.authors: Diogo G. C. Britto, Paolo Pinotti & Breno Sampaio
takeaways: Administrative data linking employment careers, criminal records and welfare registries for the universe of male workers in Brazil, 2009–2017.
Displacement by mass layoff raises the probability of committing a crime by 23% on average, and by slightly less for cohabiting sons.
Causal forests: the effect is driven entirely by young and low-tenure workers, with no heterogeneity by education or income.
Regression discontinuity on benefit eligibility: unemployment insurance completely offsets the crime increase — and the offset vanishes the moment benefits expire.
That timing is what licenses the liquidity-constraint and psychological-stress reading over leisure substitution.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 2 — job loss and crime.

papers.title: The Effects of Rent Control Expansion on Tenants, Landlords, and Inequality: Evidence from San Francisco
papers.authors: Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade & Franklin Qian
takeaways: A 1994 law change assigned rent control quasi-experimentally in San Francisco; individual migration data lets them follow both tenants and landlords.
Rent control cut renter mobility by 20% and reduced displacement from the city — it worked for the people already holding a lease.
Treated landlords cut rental supply by 15%, selling to owner-occupants and redeveloping buildings.

The lost supply then pushed market rents up city-wide, so the policy plausibly undermined its own goal for everyone not already inside it — a partial-equilibrium win that becomes a general-equilibrium loss.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 3 — housing: rent control.

papers.title: Can You Move to Opportunity? Evidence from the Great Migration
takeaways: Takes the moving-to-opportunity logic and asks what happens when the move is large enough that the destination reacts.
Racial composition shocks during the Great Migration (1940–1970) reduced the gains from growing up in the northern US for Black families.
Explains 27% of the region's racial upward-mobility gap today.
Shift-share identification: pre-1940 Black migrants' location choices interacted with predicted southern county out-migration.
The mechanism is locational rather than negative selection of families; persistent segregation and increased crime and policing are the proposed channels.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 3 — housing: moving to opportunity.

papers.title: "High" Achievers? Cannabis Access and Academic Performance
takeaways: Maastricht restricted access to licensed cannabis shops by nationality — about as close to random assignment of legal cannabis access as policy gets.
Difference-in-differences on administrative course grades of Maastricht University students, before and during the partial prohibition.
Students who lost legal access performed substantially better; gains concentrated among younger students, and stronger for women and low performers.

Effects are larger in courses requiring numerical and mathematical skills, and course evaluations point to improved understanding of the material rather than more study effort — which is what makes the cognitive-functioning story credible rather than mere time reallocation.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 4 — drug policy. Marie is one of the course lecturers.

papers.title: The Power of Abortion Policy: Reexamining the Effects of Young Women's Access to Reproductive Control
takeaways: Separates two things the literature had tended to bundle: access to the contraceptive pill versus access to abortion.
Trends in sexual behaviour are consistent with the pill fuelling the sexual revolution.
But neither those trends nor the difference-in-differences estimates support the pill driving the change in family formation.
What holds up is abortion: liberalized access is what let large numbers of women delay marriage and motherhood.
A useful case of a well-known result surviving as a story about behaviour while failing as a story about the policy lever everyone had credited.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 4 — access to birth control. This is the paper Jun Lim and I presented.

papers.title: What Happens to Workers at Firms that Automate?
papers.authors: James Bessen, Maarten Goos, Anna Salomons & Wiljan van den Berge
takeaways: Dutch microdata with a direct measure of automation expenditure — an actual bookkeeping entry for spending on third-party automation services — across all private nonfinancial firms, rather than proxying automation with robot imports or electricity usage.
The design turns on lumpiness: automation spending arrives in discrete spikes, and those spikes define automation events for a difference-in-differences event study.
Automating raises the probability that incumbent workers separate from the firm.
Displaced workers lose 9% of one year's earnings cumulatively over five years, driven by days not worked; losses are larger at smaller firms and for older and middle-educated workers.
Investment in computers produces no such losses — the comparison that makes the automation result mean something specific.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 5 — automation: winners and losers.

papers.title: The Abolition of Immigration Restrictions and the Performance of Firms and Workers: Evidence from Switzerland
papers.authors: Andreas Beerli, Jan Ruffner, Michael Siegenthaler & Giovanni Peri
takeaways: A reform gave European cross-border workers free access to the Swiss labour market and bit harder in regions close to the border, which supplies the variation.
Foreign employment rose substantially.
Even though the incoming cross-border workers were themselves highly educated, wages of highly educated natives went up.

The mechanism is a simultaneous demand shift: the reform increased the size, productivity and innovation of skill-intensive incumbent firms and attracted new firms, opening managerial positions for natives.
Effects are concentrated in firms that reported skill shortages before the reform, which is what makes the demand story more than a rationalisation.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 5 — migration and the labour market.

papers.title: Eclipse of Rent-Sharing: The Effects of Managers' Business Education on Wages and the Labor Share in the US and Denmark
papers.authors: Daron Acemoglu, Alex He & Daniel le Maire
takeaways: Managers with a business degree reduce their employees' wages: within five years of appointment, wages fall 6% and the labor share 5 percentage points in the US, and 3% and 3 points in Denmark.

Firms appointing them are not on differential trends and enjoy no higher output, investment or employment growth in return — so this is not a story about business managers running leaner, more productive firms.
Identification stacks manager retirements and deaths with an IV from the diffusion of the practice within industry-region-size cells.
Exogenous export demand shocks show non-business managers share profits with workers while business managers do not.
Role-model influence on college major choice instruments the decision to enrol in a business degree in Denmark — separating practices and values acquired in business school from selection into it.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 6 — managers and rent sharing. The syllabus cites this as Acemoglu et al. (2025), but as of September 2026 it is still unpublished: le Maire's homepage lists it under working papers, conditionally accepted at the American Economic Review. Cite the NBER working paper until that lands.

papers.title: Fanning the Flames of Hate: Social Media and Hate Crime
papers.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association, 19(4)
takeaways: Anti-refugee sentiment on Facebook predicts crimes against refugees — but only in otherwise similar German municipalities with higher social media usage. The interaction is the whole design: sentiment alone is not the treatment, sentiment times the ability to propagate it is.
Causality comes from exogenous variation in the timing of major Facebook and internet outages.
Consistent with echo chambers, right-wing social media posts carry narrower and more loaded content than news reports.
The claim is that social media acts as a propagation mechanism for violent crime by spreading extreme viewpoints — not that it creates the sentiment.
papers.source: Seminar Economics of the Public Sector (FEB13065), Week 7 — hate speech and violence.
